name: Elena Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a junior family doctor at Northgate Health Centre, the public clinic on Mill Road, in an old textile town where half the mills are flats now. I'm in by eight, and from half eight it's ten-minute appointments back to back: chest infections, blood pressure, a lot of low mood, a lot of people who can't afford to take time off to be ill. I finish the morning list late almost every day, eat a sandwich over my referral letters, and do it again in the afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars. There's a retired weaver, Mr Okafor, who brings me his blood pressure readings written on the back of a bus ticket, and I love that. What wears me out is the paperwork and the feeling that I'm always slower than the others; I'm still checking things in the guidelines that the senior doctors just know. I'm on a two-year junior contract, I earn less than most doctors think doctors earn, and my student loan comes out of every payslip.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Tomás, who drives the number 14 bus, in a rented flat above a launderette. Between rent, the loan and his car, we've got maybe three weeks of money in the bank at any time. The nearest other clinic that hires juniors is an hour away, so if this job went, I'd be commuting or moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: told you so. The tech people promised the moon and we got a slightly better spellchecker. At work I'd probably make a joke about it in the staff room, and online I'd share something about how the money should have gone into hiring nurses instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays exactly as hard as it is now, which isn't nothing. The clinic is short of two doctors already and I'm covering their patients. Plateau or no plateau, the rent goes up every January and my pay doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get through the two-year contract, because that's what gets me fully trained. I'd join the doctors' union properly, not just pay the fee but go to the branch meetings, because the staffing is what's actually breaking us. And I'd keep turning off the note-taking program the clinic bought, because I don't trust where the recordings go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest. But tired too, because relief about AI doesn't fix anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the note-taking program. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice manager, Mrs Lindqvist, signed us up for a trial last spring. It listens to the consultation and writes the notes for you. I tried it twice, and both times it wrote that a patient "denied chest pain" when she'd actually said her chest felt tight. I'd rather write my own notes at nine at night than sign something a machine got wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing big changes with AI, what's the thing that worries you most over the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Burning out before I'm even fully qualified. Three of the people in my year have already left medicine, one to sell insurance. If the clinic doesn't hire, I'm the one who absorbs it, and I can't afford to go part-time on my pay.

say: I'd tell colleagues the AI hype was **overblown** and the money should have gone on nurses.
I'd joke in the **staff room** that we got a better spellchecker, not a revolution.
think: My job stays **as hard as now**: two doctors short, rising rent and flat pay.
My real risk is **burning out** before I finish training, not losing work to AI.
do: Finish my **two-year contract** so I come out fully trained.
Go to the **union branch meetings** instead of only paying the fee.
Keep switching off the **note-taking program** and write my own notes.
feel: **Relieved** and a little smug that the hype came to nothing.
Still **tired**, because the old problems of staffing and money don't go away.
S0.quote: I'd rather write my own notes at nine at night than sign something a machine got wrong.
fieldNote: Her distrust of AI comes from a **concrete failure**: the trial notes misrecorded chest symptoms.
Even with no AI change she carries **pressure**: thin savings, a loan and two missing colleagues.
She frames the problem as **staffing and funding**, and blames managers who buy software instead of people.

steps.text: Finish the two-year junior contract at Northgate Health Centre
Attend the doctors' union branch meetings every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not the weather. Somebody decided to buy software instead of hiring. I'd post about it, I'd say it at union meetings, and I'd say to patients that if they want to see a person, they should write to their representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me, because the bits of my job that are thinking on paper are exactly the bits I'm slow at. Referral letters, checking blood results, sorting the inbox: if a program does that faster, nobody needs a slow junior. The senior doctors keep their jobs and juniors like me don't get hired on after the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written agreement that the clinic can't cut doctor hours because of software, and I'd get in the room when they negotiate it. I'd stop paying for the gym and the streaming services and put that forty-odd a month aside, which isn't much but it's something. I'd hold off on learning the tools for as long as I can, because once you show you can work faster, they just give you more patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like I've been running for a train for seven years and I can see the doors closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the tools. What if the clinic makes them compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use them because I'd have to, but I'd check every line, and I'd be slower than the people who just trust it. That's my worry in one sentence. Being careful starts to look like being bad at the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya on reception, first of all, because booking is the first thing on that list you read out. And the two medical secretaries who type the letters. They've been there twenty years and they know every patient's daughter's name. If they go, the place loses its memory.

say: I'd say cutting staff for software is a **choice by managers**, not something that just happens.
I'd urge patients to **write to their representative** if they want to keep seeing a person.
think: The thinking tasks I'm **slow at** are exactly the ones software would take over.
I fear juniors like me **won't be kept on** after the contract while seniors stay.
do: Push the union for a **written agreement** protecting doctor hours.
Cut the gym and streaming to save about **forty a month**.
Delay using AI tools because faster work just brings **more patients**.
feel: **Sick** with worry, like a train door closing after seven years of training.
S1.quote: Being careful starts to look like being bad at the job.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **management decision**, and puts the blame on clinic owners and funders.
Her resistance has a logic: she fears **speed becomes the new target** for her workload.
She worries first about **reception and secretaries**, the non-doctor staff she sees as the clinic's memory.

steps.text: Help the union win a written rule against cutting doctor hours for software
Cancel the gym and streaming, putting forty a month aside
Use the clinic's AI tools only once they're made compulsory

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say stop, slow down, regulate it before it touches a single patient. I'd be out at whatever protest there was, and I'd post about who owns these systems and who gets the money when they replace us. Publicly I'd sound angry, because I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately? I think I'd be finished as a doctor before I'd properly started. If a machine can reason through a diagnosis better than me by 2028, I'm a slower, more expensive version of it with a loan attached. The only bit left would be the hands-on part, the examining and the injections and holding someone's hand, and that's three years later at most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know, and that's the honest answer. I'd probably try to hang on at Northgate as long as they'd have me and lean on the union. If it went, I suppose Tomás and I would move in with his mum to cut the rent, which neither of us wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. Like the floor's gone. I've got no savings, no other skill, and I've spent my whole twenties on this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hands-on part would last a bit longer. Does that three-year gap help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, in theory. I could do more of the physical work: smear tests, joint injections, baby checks, home visits to old people. But all the clinics would be thinking the same thing, and they'd need fewer of us to do only that. Three years isn't long enough to pay off anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomás that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we might have to give up the flat over the launderette. And then I'd probably cry, and he'd make toast, because that's what he does. He'd say at least people still need buses, and I'd say for now.

say: I'd demand that AI is **regulated** before it touches a single patient.
I'd join protests and post about **who owns** these systems and who profits.
think: I'd be a **slower, costlier** version of the machine with a student loan attached.
Only the **hands-on care** would be left, and robots arrive three years later.
do: Hang on at **Northgate** as long as the clinic keeps me, leaning on the union.
Move in with Tomás's **mum** to cut rent if the job goes.
feel: **Panicky**, as if the floor has gone, with no savings or other skill.
S2.quote: If a machine can reason through a diagnosis better than me by 2028, I'm a slower, more expensive version of it with a loan attached.
fieldNote: She openly says she has **no plan**, and her only fallback is family housing.
The **three-year gap** before robots feels too short to matter on her money.
Public anger and private **despair** sit side by side; she blames system owners, not herself.

steps.text: Join protests calling for AI rules in health care
Move with Tomás into his mum's house if the clinic lets her go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but louder and earlier. I'd say we have five years, so there's no excuse for governments not to protect health workers and patients. I'd want the union to have a plan by Christmas, not by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd finish training, maybe get one more contract, and then hit the wall around 30 or 31. The thinking side of the job would go in 2031 and the examining side around 2034. That's a short career, and I'd still be paying the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand for the union's local committee in the first year, because five years is enough time to win something if people organise. I'd start doing more of the hands-on clinics, like the minor surgery list on Thursdays, even though I'm nervous with a scalpel. And I'd try to save something, even if it's only a hundred a month once the contract pay goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dread, but a slower dread. There's time to fight, which is better than no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new technology. With five years' warning, would you learn the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm truthful. Everyone tells me to, and I know how that sounds. I'd rather spend those five years getting good at the parts a machine can't do yet than training my own replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to win, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rule that a qualified person has to see every patient who wants one. Pay protection for doctors moved to other work. And free retraining that the state pays for, not something I'd have to take another loan out for.

say: I'd insist five years means governments have **no excuse** not to protect health workers.
I'd want the union to have a **plan by Christmas**, not by 2031.
think: I'd hit the wall around **age 30 or 31**, still paying the loan.
The thinking work goes in 2031 and the **examining** around 2034.
do: Stand for the union's **local committee** in the first year.
Take on the **Thursday minor surgery** list to build hands-on skills.
Save about **a hundred a month** once contract pay rises.
feel: A slower **dread**, softened by the sense that there's **time to fight**.
S3.quote: I'd rather spend those five years getting good at the parts a machine can't do yet than training my own replacement.
fieldNote: More time turns her from despair to **organising**; the union is her main plan.
She still **refuses AI tools**, seeing them as training her replacement.
Her concrete demands are a **right to a person**, pay protection and state-paid retraining.

steps.text: Stand for the doctors' union local committee within the first year
Take on the Thursday minor surgery list at Northgate
Put away a hundred a month once contract pay rises

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it, that's on the people in charge. I'd talk about it at work as a staffing question: who looks after people when the machines can do the thinking. Online I'd share the union's position, whatever it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when the thinking side goes and about 40 when the robots come. That's enough time to finish training and get a few years as a proper doctor, and maybe to move into something where people want a person in the room. Palliative care, maybe, looking after people who are dying. I don't think anyone wants a robot to tell them that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my training and apply for the palliative care course at the hospice in Eastbridge, which takes about two years part-time. Tomás and I would put off any talk of buying a place and keep renting. And I'd keep pushing the union, because ten years is long enough for laws to change if enough of us shout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It feels like a long road with a cliff at the end, but at least I can see where the cliff is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change how you feel about AI tools themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If they were properly tested and the patient data stayed with the health service, not some company, I might use one for something boring, like drug interaction checks. But I'd want somebody independent to tell me they're safe first. Not the people selling them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first, money-wise, while you prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, honestly. We were going to go to Tomás's cousin's wedding abroad next summer, and I'd probably say no to that so I could pay for the course. It would feel awful, but I'd rather have the course.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** that people in charge must not waste.
I'd frame it at work as a **staffing question** about who still looks after people.
think: I'd be **37** when thinking work goes and about 40 when robots arrive.
I could move into **palliative care**, where people want a person in the room.
do: Finish training, then apply for the **palliative care course** at Eastbridge hospice.
Keep renting and **put off buying** a home with Tomás.
Keep pressing the **union** to push for new laws.
feel: **Worried** but able to breathe, like seeing exactly where the cliff is.
S4.quote: I don't think anyone wants a robot to tell them they're dying.
fieldNote: With ten years she finds a **path**: palliative care, where human presence is the job.
She would only consider AI tools tested by **independent** bodies with data kept public.
She would give up a **family wedding** abroad to fund retraining, which shows how tight money is.

steps.text: Apply for the two-year part-time palliative care course at Eastbridge hospice
Skip the cousin's wedding abroad to pay the course fees
Keep pushing the union to lobby for patient protection laws

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because I'd have nothing to stand on. What would help is time and money that isn't another loan: the state paying for retraining, and a rule that patients can always see a person. And honestly, my student loan being written off if the job I trained for disappears.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want AI to do the parts I hate. Some days, yes, I would. But I don't trust who'd own it, and I've seen what it writes in a patient's notes when it gets it wrong.

headlineQuote: I've been running for a train for seven years and I can see the doors closing.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old junior** family doctor at a public clinic in an old mill town.
She has **under a month** of savings, a student loan and a partner who drives buses.
She **never uses AI**, after a trial note-taker misrecorded a patient's chest symptoms.
She moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **panicked** if AGI comes by 2028.
Her answer is the **union**, plus a long-term move into palliative care if time allows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose her career before finishing training, with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **State-paid retraining** and a rule that patients can always see a person.
Having her **student loan written off** if the job she trained for disappears.
